questions.q: Display the message Hello world.

teach.say: print() puts one line on the screen. The text goes inside the brackets, in quotation marks.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Nothing else is printed.
questions.starter: # Print one line

tests.why: Nothing was printed. Text goes inside print( ) and inside quotation marks.

questions.fb: That is a whole program: print() shows one line, and the quotation marks say where the text starts and ends.

questions.q: Display Open. Then display Closed on the next line.

teach.say: One print() gives one line, and then Python moves down. Two lines of output need two print() statements, in the order you want them.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Print exactly: Open
Print exactly: Closed
questions.starter: # Print two lines, one after the other

tests.why: Two lines of output needs two print() statements, and they run in the order you write them.

questions.fb: Each print() ends by moving down to the next line, which is why printing twice gives two lines.

questions.q: Display Top. Then display an empty line. Then display Bottom on the third line.

teach.say: print() with nothing inside the brackets prints a line with nothing on it.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
The second line of output has nothing on it.
Three lines of output in all.
questions.starter: # Three lines, with the middle one empty

tests.why: The empty line is printed on purpose, with print() and nothing in the brackets. Two lines of output means it is missing.

questions.fb: An empty print() still counts as a line of output, which is how you leave a gap.

questions.q: Display Line 1 of 2. Then display Done! on the next line.

teach.say: Digits and punctuation inside the quotation marks are part of the text, and print() shows them exactly as written.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Print exactly: Line 1 of 2
Print exactly: Done!
questions.starter: # Two lines of text, digits and punctuation included

tests.why: Copy both lines exactly, the digits and the exclamation mark included. Inside quotation marks a digit is text, not a number to work out.

questions.fb: Inside quotation marks everything is text, so a digit or a full stop is just another character to show.

questions.q: Keep the word harbour in a variable. Display that variable. Then display it again on the next line.

teach.say: A variable is a named box. = puts a value into it, and printing the name shows the value inside.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
The word harbour is written into your program.
Print the same variable twice.
questions.starter: # One word in a variable, printed on two lines

tests.why: Two lines, both the same. One line means the variable was printed once: printing it does not use the value up.

questions.fb: A variable is a named box for one value, and the value stays in the box until you change it.

questions.q: Keep the word north in a variable. Display that variable. Then change the variable to the word south. Display it again on the next line.

teach.say: = replaces whatever the variable held before, so only the newest value is left. Print the old value before you overwrite it.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Use one variable for both words.
Print the first word before the second one replaces it.
questions.starter: # One variable, printed twice, with a new value in between

tests.why: If south came out on both lines, the first print() runs after the change. A second = throws the old value away, so print it first.

questions.fb: A variable holds one value at a time, and = overwrites whatever was there before.

questions.q: Keep the word amber in a variable called a. Copy the value of a into a second variable called b. Then change a to the word silver. Display a. Then display b on the next line.

teach.say: b = a copies across the value a is holding at that moment. Changing a afterwards leaves b exactly as it was.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
b = a copies the value, so b keeps the word amber.
Print a first, then b.
questions.starter: # Copy one variable into another before changing it

tests.why: If both lines are silver, b was copied after a changed. Copy it while a still holds amber.

questions.fb: Copying a variable copies the value, not the box, so the copy keeps that value even after the original changes.

questions.q: Keep the word closed in a variable. Keep the whole number 100 in a constant called LIMIT. Display the variable. Then display LIMIT on the next line.

teach.say: A constant is a variable whose value never changes. Its name is written in capitals so everyone can see it must stay as it is.

brief: Nothing is typed in by the user.
Name the constant LIMIT, in capitals.
The 100 is written into your program in one place only.
questions.starter: # Make the variable and the constant, then print both

tests.why: Two lines: the word, then the number. If the word LIMIT appeared, it was inside quotation marks, and quotation marks mean print these letters.

questions.fb: A constant is an ordinary variable for a value that must not change, and capital letters are how programmers say so.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Display [word].

teach.say: input() stops the program and waits for the user to type a line, then hands that line back. Keep it in a variable, and printing the variable shows what was typed.
code: colour = input("Colour? ")   # the user types teal

brief: The user types in one word.
Keep what comes back in a variable.
Nothing else is printed.
questions.starter: # Read one word into a variable, then print it

tests.why: Nothing came out, so the typed word was never printed. input() hands the word back and print() shows it.
If the word word came out instead, the variable was inside quotation marks. Quotation marks mean print these letters.
input() hands back the whole line, spaces included, so both words come back as one value.

questions.fb: input() reads one line and hands it back, and printing a variable shows the value it is holding.

questions.q: Ask the user for one word. Display [word]. Then display [word] again on the next line. Then display [word] a third time on the next line.

teach.say: A value read with input() stays in its variable after it has been printed, so you can use it as many times as you like.
code: sound = input("Sound? ")   # the user types beep

brief: The user types in one word only.
questions.starter: # Read the word, then print it three times

tests.why: Three lines exactly. One line means the value was printed once; nothing at all means input() was never stored in a variable.
input() reads the whole line, spaces included, so both words come back as one value.
Reading again instead of printing the variable three times will not work: there is only one line of input.

questions.fb: input() waits for one line and hands it back, and once it is stored you can use it as often as you like.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Display [second word]. Then display [first word] on the next line.

teach.say: One input() reads one line, so two lines need two calls. Each value goes in its own variable, and then you print them in any order.
code: a = input("First? ")   # the user types red

brief: The user types in two lines, one word on each.
Print the second word first.
questions.starter: # Two words in, two lines out, the second word first

tests.why: The first word arrives first but is printed second, so store each input in its own variable and then choose the order.
One input() reads one line only. Two lines of input need two separate calls.
Using one variable for both words loses the first one, because the second input overwrites it.

questions.fb: Reading and printing are separate steps, so once each value is in its own variable you can print them in any order.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Display [first word]. Then display [second word] on the next line. Then display [first word] again on the next line. Then display [second word] again on the next line.

teach.say: Both variables are still there after they have been printed, so you can print either of them again.
code: a = input("First? ")   # the user types red

brief: The user types in two lines, one word on each.
Four lines of output from two words.
questions.starter: # Two words in, four lines out, taking turns

tests.why: Four lines exactly. Two lines means the pair was printed once instead of twice.
Reading again for the third and fourth lines will not work: there are only two lines of input.
The order matters: first word, second word, first word, second word.

questions.fb: Printing a variable does not use the value up, so the same two variables can fill as many lines as you like.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word and keep it in its own variable. Then ask for a second word and keep it in its own variable. Then ask for a third word and keep it in its own variable. Display [third word]. Then display [first word] on the next line. Then display [second word] on the next line.

teach.say: Three values need three variables, and each one keeps whatever was put in it whatever order you print them in.
code: a = input("First? ")   # the user types red

brief: The user types in three lines, one word on each.
Print them in the order given, not the order they were typed.
questions.starter: # Three words in. Third, first, second.

tests.why: The third word comes out first, then the first, then the second. Printing them as typed gets all three lines wrong.
Three inputs need three separate input() calls, each stored in its own variable.
Reusing one variable for all three words leaves only the last one, so the first two lines cannot be printed.

questions.fb: Each variable holds its own value, so reading in one order and printing in another is just a matter of choosing which to print first.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Display one line in the form Word is [word].

teach.say: The + sign joins text together. It adds nothing of its own, so any space you want has to be joined in too.

brief: One line only.
There is one space between is and the word.
questions.starter: # Join the fixed text to the word, then print one line

tests.why: Word istulip means the space is missing. Joining never adds spaces for you, so put one inside the quotation marks.
Two lines instead of one means two print() statements. Build the whole line, then print it once.
If the word word appeared on the end, the variable was inside the quotation marks. Only the fixed text belongs in quotes.

questions.fb: Joining text with + is called concatenation, and it joins exactly what you give it, so every space is joined in on purpose.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a second word. Join them with one space between them. Display one line in the form [first word] [second word].

teach.say: Two variables can be joined the same way as text and a variable, as long as the space between them is joined in as well.

brief: One line only.
Exactly one space between the two words.
No other text is printed.
questions.starter: # Two words in, one joined line out

tests.why: deepwater means the space is missing. Join it in on purpose: first + " " + second.
Two lines instead of one means both words were printed separately. Join them first, then print once.
Printing the variable names instead of their values means they were inside quotation marks.

questions.fb: Concatenation joins values end to end, so a space between two words is something you have to supply yourself.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Display [word]. Then display the whole number 7 on the next line. Then display the real number 1.5 on the next line.

teach.say: Python values come in types: text in quotation marks is a string, 4 is an integer and 0.5 is a real number.

brief: The 7 and the 1.5 are fixed in your program, not typed in.
A number printed on its own needs no quotation marks.
questions.starter: # A string, then an integer, then a real number

tests.why: Three lines, each with one value. 1.50 or 1 point 5 are strings that look like numbers and will not match.
7.0 instead of 7 means the integer was written as a real number. An integer has no decimal part at all.
The word comes from input() and the two numbers are written straight into the program.

questions.fb: Integer, real, Boolean, character and string are the five data types OCR names, and the type decides what you can do with a value.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Display [word]. Then display the Boolean True on the next line. Then display the Boolean False on the next line.

teach.say: A Boolean holds one of only two values. They are written True and False, with a capital letter and no quotation marks.

brief: True and False are fixed in your program, not typed in.
Write them with a capital letter and no quotation marks.
questions.starter: # A string, then the two Boolean values

tests.why: Three lines, in that order. true or TRUE is not how Python writes it: the capital letter is on the first letter only.
In quotation marks it is only a string that looks like a Boolean. Leave the quotes off so Python prints the Boolean itself.
The word comes from input(). The two Boolean values are written straight into the program.

questions.fb: A Boolean is either True or False, written with a capital letter and never in quotation marks.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Add 1 to it. Display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: input() always hands back text, and arithmetic needs a number. int() turns the text into a whole number first.
code: count = int(input("How many? "))   # the user types 6

brief: The user types in one whole number.
Cast it with int() before adding.
questions.starter: # One whole number in, one more out

tests.why: 141 instead of 15 means the 1 was joined on as text. Wrap the input in int() before adding.
0 plus 1 is 1. An empty line means nothing was printed, so the arithmetic is missing.
Print the answer, not the number that was typed in. The 1 has to be added before printing.

questions.fb: Casting with int() turns a string of digits into a whole number you can do arithmetic with.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number. Add them together. Display [total] and nothing else.

teach.say: + adds two numbers but joins two strings, so each input has to be cast with int() before you add them.

brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, one total out

tests.why: 147 is the giveaway: + joined two strings instead of adding them. Wrap each one in int(input()).
Cast before adding, not after. int(input()) + int(input()) works; adding first joins the text.
A 0 is still a number to be read, so both lines must be read, in order.

questions.fb: The same + means two different things, and which one you get depends entirely on the type of the values either side of it.

questions.q: Ask the user for a number, which may have a decimal point. Display [number] as a real number and nothing else, so 4 shows as 4.0.

teach.say: float() turns text into a real number, and a real number always keeps a decimal part, so 2 becomes 2.0.

brief: The user types in one number, which may have a decimal point.
Cast it with float(), not int().
questions.starter: # Read the number, make it a real number, print it

tests.why: A crash here means int() was used, and int() cannot handle a decimal point.
4 instead of 4.0 means the text was printed as it was typed, or int() was used. float() always keeps a decimal part.
Print the variable you cast, not the line that came back from input().

questions.fb: float() casts text to a real number, which always has a decimal part even when the value is whole.

questions.q: Ask the user for a number, which may have a decimal point. Display one line in the form Value is [number], with the number as a real number, so 4 shows as 4.0.

teach.say: str() turns a number back into text so that + will join it to a message.

brief: The user types in one number, which may have a decimal point.
Cast it in with float().
Cast it back with str() to join it to the text.
questions.starter: # Read the number, make it real, print the line

tests.why: A crash here is joining a number to text with +. Cast it back with str() first.
4 instead of 4.0 means int() was used, or the text went straight in. float() always shows a decimal part.
Value is on its own line means two print() statements. Build one line, then print it once.

questions.fb: float() casts text to a real number and str() casts a number back to text, and one line of output often needs both.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Add 1 to the number. Display [word]. Then display [answer] on the next line.

teach.say: Read each value, cast the ones you need as numbers, then print the answers in the order the question asks for.
code: team = input("Team? ")   # the user types Owls

brief: The user types in two lines: a word, then a whole number.
Only the number is cast with int().
The word stays as text.
questions.starter: # A word and a number in. The word, then one more.

tests.why: 31 on the second line means the number was still text, so the 1 was joined on the end. Cast with int() before adding.
0 plus 1 is 1. An empty second line means the arithmetic is missing.
Casting the word with int() crashes. Only the value you are doing arithmetic on needs casting.

questions.fb: A program can hold text and numbers at the same time, and you cast only the values you are going to calculate with.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Add 1 to the number. Display one line in the form [word] [answer], with one space between them.

teach.say: A number cannot be joined to text with + until str() has turned it back into text.
code: n = int(input("How many? "))   # the user types 4

brief: The user types in two lines: a word, then a whole number.
One line of output.
Exactly one space between the word and the answer.
questions.starter: # A word and a number in, one joined line out

tests.why: A crash here is joining a number to text with +. Cast the answer back with str().
0 plus 1 is 1, and it still has to be joined on the end of the word.
silver11 means the space is missing, and silver 111 means the 1 was joined on as text instead of added.

questions.fb: Casting runs both ways in the same program: int() on the way in so you can calculate, str() on the way out so you can join.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number. Add them together. Display one line in the form Total: [total].

teach.say: Cast on the way in with int() so the arithmetic works, and on the way out with str() so the joining works.

brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
Print exactly: Total:
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, one line of answer out

tests.why: Total: 147 means the two inputs were joined as text. Cast each one with int() before adding.
A 0 is still a number to be read, so both lines must be read, in order.
A crash here is joining the total to the text with + before str() has turned it back into text.

questions.fb: Nearly every program casts twice: int() to calculate with the input, str() to put the answer into a sentence.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Then ask for a second whole number. Add the two numbers together. Display [word]. Then display Total: [total] on the next line.

teach.say: Most programs are this shape: read the inputs, cast each one to the type you need, work something out, then print it in the form asked for.
code: label = input("Label? ")   # the user types North

brief: The user types in three lines: a word, then two whole numbers.
Print exactly: Total:
The word is printed on its own line, above the total.
questions.starter: # A word and two numbers in. The word, then the total.

tests.why: Total: 147 means the two numbers were joined as text. Cast each one with int() before adding.
Three lines of input are read in the order the question gives, so the word is read first.
One line of output means the word and the total were joined together. They go on separate lines.

questions.fb: Read, cast, calculate, print: every program in this course is some version of those four steps.
